newsitem.title: CANADA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-HASEK DOMINATES SUBDUED NHL AWARDS CEREMONY.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-HASEK DOMINATES SUBDUED NHL AWARDS CEREMONY.

text.p: Brilliant Buffalo goaltender Dominik Hasek and the overachieving Sabres dominated the National Hockey League awards dinner, grabbing five of the major awards handed out on Thursday.

Hasek won the league's most prestigious award, the Hart Memorial Trophy, given to the NHL player most valuable to his team. He also picked up the Vezina Trophy as the league's top goaltender and the Lester B. Pearson Award.

The Pearson award is the most valuable player honour decided in balloting by the NHL players. The other awards are determined in voting by members of the Professional Hockey Writers' Association members.
"It's a fantastic honour for me," Hasek said in accepting the Hart Trophy, which had not been awarded to a goaltender since Jacques Plante won it in 1952.
"After winning the Vezina a couple of minutes ago and the Lester Pearson earlier today, this is something I cannot describe in words."

Hasek won a career-high 37 games, with five shutouts and a goals-against average of 2.27 in backstopping the surprising Sabres to the Northeast Division title. He also led the league in save percentage (.930) for the fourth year in a row.
This was Hasek's third Vezina Trophy in four years.
Hasek beat out Colorado's Patrick Roy and Martin Brodeur of the New Jersey Devils for the Vezina.

This year's NHL awards banquet was far less festive than usual with Detroit Red Wings defenceman Vladimir Konstantinov hospitalized in a coma instead of in attendance as one of the finalists for the Norris Trophy.
"For everyone it's really put things in perspective," said the Anaheim Ducks' Paul Kariya, winner of the Lady Byng Trophy and a finalist for the Hart and Pearson awards.
Konstantinov suffered serious head injuries in a limousine crash last Friday.
"My agent has a couple of players on Detroit and he said they look at it like they won the Stanley Cup 10 years ago. It means nothing to them now," Kariya said.
"We all are concerned with Vladimir ... It really puts life into perspective and makes you take a second look at what's important in life..."
The Norris Trophy, awarded to the year's best defenceman, went to Brian Leetch of the New York Rangers, who won it for the second time in his career.

Leetch led all defenceman in scoring with 20 goals and 58 assists. In voting that took place at the end of the regular season, Leetch beat out Konstantinov and Sandis Ozolinsh of the Colorado Avalanche.
Like many of the Thursday's winners, Leetch said Konstantinov and the team's masseur Sergei Mnatsakanov, who was also in a coma, were in his thoughts.
"We're all waiting as anxiously as the next person and their families," Leetch said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with them. It's a tragedy."
New York Islanders defenceman Bryan Berard won the Calder Memorial Trophy as the NHL's top rookie.
Berard, who was second overall in rookie scoring with eight goals and 40 assists, beat Jim Campbell of the St Louis Blues and Jarome Iginla of the Calgary Flames.
Buffalo Sabres centre Mike Peca won the Frank J. Selke Trophy, given to the NHL's top defensive forward.
Peca led all Sabres with a plus-26 rating and led the NHL with six short-handed goals.
"I'm very honoured and overwhelmed by everything that's going on today," said Peca, who was chosen over Colorado centre Peter Forsberg and Dallas winger Jere Lehtinen.
Also bringing an award back to Buffalo was Sabres coach Ted Nolan, who won the Jack Adams Award the NHL's top coach.
Nolan guided the Sabres to their first division title since 1981 with a 40-30-12 record for 92 points.
"This is really unbelievable," said Nolan, who barely edged Ken Hitchcock of the Dallas Stars for the honour.
Nolan was named first on 39 ballots and finished with 307 points, while Hitchcock, who guided Dallas to the league's second best record with 104 points, received 38 first-place votes and 300 points.
Jacques Martin of the Ottawa Senators was a distant third.
The Lady Byng Trophy for sportsmanship went to Kariya for the second consecutive year.
Kariya, one of the NHL's major young talents, finished third in the league in scoring with 44 goals and 55 assists despite missing 15 games for the Mighty Ducks.
But the statistic that brought him the Lady Byng was a mere six penalty minutes all season, an amount most players can easily rack up in a single game.
Kariya and retired superstar Mario Lemieux were the losing finalists for the Hart Trophy. But the three-time Hart winner did not leave empty handed.
Lemieux had already locked up his sixth Art Ross Trophy as league's leading scorer, ending his career on top.
